relevant_findings.topic: Coating type is the primary configuration dimension — NOT quality tier
relevant_findings.finding: Deck coatings are fundamentally different from house paint. The primary dimension is coating_type: clear_sealer (12-18 month cycle, no UV pigment, wood grain fully visible), semi_transparent (2-3 year cycle, professional residential standard, pigment in carrier penetrates wood), semi_solid (3-4 year cycle, heavier pigment load, partial grain masking), solid_stain (5-7 year cycle, film-forming, complete grain masking). Semi-transparent stain is the professional standard for residential decks — it balances aesthetics, protection, and maintainability.

Clear sealers, semi-transparent stains, and semi-solid stains are PENETRATING coatings — they soak into wood fibers rather than forming a surface film. Solid stain is FILM-FORMING (builds a surface film like paint). This distinction drives completely different failure modes: penetrating coatings ERODE (wear away gradually, easy to maintain), film-forming coatings PEEL and DELAMINATE (catastrophic failure requiring full strip). On horizontal walking surfaces, film-forming coatings trap moisture from above and below, creating delamination risk.

relevant_findings.topic: No primer in penetrating stain systems
relevant_findings.finding: Penetrating stains (clear, semi-transparent, semi-solid) do NOT use primer. The stain itself penetrates directly into bare or prepared wood fibers. Primer would seal the wood surface and PREVENT stain penetration — the opposite of the desired effect. Solid stain on previously painted surfaces may require primer for adhesion, but this is an edge case. The traditional prime→paint pipeline does not apply to deck staining.

relevant_findings.topic: New pressure-treated pine requires 3-6 month seasoning
relevant_findings.finding: New pressure-treated (PT) lumber contains waterborne preservatives (ACQ, CA-B, MCA) that leave the wood saturated with copper-based compounds and moisture. Wood must season 3-6 months before staining to allow preservatives to cure and moisture content to drop below 15%. Staining green PT wood results in poor penetration, blotchy appearance, and premature coating failure. This is a HARD STOP if wood age is less than 3 months — do not coat.

relevant_findings.topic: Mill glaze removal mandatory on new wood
relevant_findings.finding: New lumber (especially PT pine and cedar) has mill glaze — a burnished, shiny surface created by planing at the sawmill. Mill glaze seals the wood surface and prevents stain penetration. MUST be removed before staining. Removal methods: chemical mill glaze remover (preferred) or mechanical sanding with 60-80 grit. Mill glaze removal is a mandatory prep task for all new wood substrates regardless of coating type.

Maximum moisture content for deck wood before staining is 15% (measured by electronic pin-type moisture meter). MC above 15% is a HARD STOP — stain will not penetrate properly and will fail prematurely. Water bead test (sprinkle water on surface — if it beads, wood is not ready; if it absorbs within 30 seconds, wood is ready to accept stain) is a field-expedient supplement but electronic meter reading is the authoritative measurement.

Weathered decks (UV-degraded, grayed, loose fiber) require a three-step chemical restoration protocol: (1) Alkaline strip/cleaner — removes failed coating residue, mildew, dirt, opens wood pores. Sodium hydroxide or sodium percarbonate based. (2) Acid brightener — restores natural wood color by dissolving surface tannin deposits and neutralizing alkaline residue. Oxalic acid for cedar/redwood tannin, citric acid as alternative. (3) Neutralize and rinse — thorough water rinse to remove all chemical residue. Allow 24-48 hours drying before staining.

relevant_findings.topic: Cedar and redwood tannin bleed management
relevant_findings.finding: Cedar and redwood contain water-soluble extractive tannins that bleed through coatings, causing dark brown/red discoloration. Tannin bleed is most severe with water-based coatings and on end-grain. Oxalic acid brightener treatment before staining dissolves surface tannins. Oil-based stains resist tannin bleed better than water-based. For clear/semi-transparent coatings, some tannin bleed is aesthetically acceptable (natural wood look). For solid stain, tannin-blocking primer may be required.

relevant_findings.topic: Solid stain delamination risk on horizontal surfaces
relevant_findings.finding: Solid stain (film-forming) on horizontal walking surfaces is a documented high-risk application. Horizontal surfaces collect standing water from rain, snow, and irrigation. Water penetrates through cracks, end-grain, and fastener holes, becomes trapped under the film, and causes blistering and sheet delamination. Foot traffic abrades the film further. Professional recommendation: semi-transparent or semi-solid stain preferred for horizontal deck surfaces. If solid stain is specified, document the delamination risk warning and shorter maintenance cycle.

relevant_findings.topic: Back-brushing mandatory when spraying penetrating stains
relevant_findings.finding: Spray application of penetrating stains on decks REQUIRES back-brushing (not back-rolling). Spray deposits stain on the surface but does not force it into wood pores. Back-brushing with a stiff synthetic bristle brush works stain into the wood grain, ensuring proper penetration and even absorption. This is similar in concept to masonry backroll but uses a brush instead of a roller because wood grain requires bristle action for stain penetration. Spray-only application of penetrating stains is NOT acceptable.

A deck is not a single surface — it is a multi-component structure requiring item-level estimation: (1) Deck floor field (SF) — main walking surface, largest area, highest wear. (2) Railings (LF) — top rail, bottom rail, posts, measured linearly. (3) Spindles/balusters (EA) — individual turned or square members, counted per piece, high labor intensity per unit. (4) Stairs (EA per step) — each tread+riser is one unit, high-detail work, end-grain exposure. Each component has different production rates, access conditions, and coating consumption.

relevant_findings.topic: UV degradation and lignin photodegradation on horizontal surfaces
relevant_findings.finding: Unprotected wood exposed to UV radiation undergoes photodegradation of lignin (the natural binder between cellulose fibers). UV breaks down lignin, leaving behind silvery-gray cellulose. Horizontal deck surfaces receive maximum UV exposure (direct overhead sun). UV degradation is the primary driver of coating erosion on decks — clear sealers fail fastest (12-18 months) because they have no UV-blocking pigment. Each step up in pigment load (semi-transparent → semi-solid → solid) provides longer UV protection.

relevant_findings.topic: Composite decking exclusion from primary scope
relevant_findings.finding: Composite decking (Trex, TimberTech, Fiberon, etc.) is manufactured as a maintenance-free, factory-colored product and is generally NOT stained or painted by professional painting contractors. Composite decking manufacturers explicitly void warranties if coated. Painting composite is a rare edge case (homeowner wants color change) with specialized adhesion requirements. EXCLUDE composite from primary scope of this spec — note as edge-case-only with separate adhesion protocol if ever needed.

relevant_findings.topic: Maintenance cycle expectations by coating type
relevant_findings.finding: Deck coatings have dramatically shorter maintenance cycles than house paint (which lasts 10-15+ years). Clear sealer: 12-18 months (annual maintenance). Semi-transparent: 2-3 years. Semi-solid: 3-4 years. Solid stain: 5-7 years (but delamination risk on horizontal). These cycles are driven by horizontal UV exposure, foot traffic abrasion, and water pooling — conditions vertical surfaces do not face. Maintenance recoat of penetrating stains is simple (clean and recoat) vs. solid stain (strip, sand, recoat).

condition_drivers.impact: PRIMARY CONFIGURATION DIMENSION. Drives coating chemistry (penetrating vs film-forming), maintenance cycle, failure mode profile, primer requirement (none for penetrating, possible for solid), material coverage rates, and UV protection level. Replaces quality_tier as the primary dimension for this spec.
condition_drivers.notes: Semi-transparent is the professional standard default. Solid stain triggers delamination risk warning on horizontal surfaces.

condition_drivers.impact: Drives prep module selection. New: mill glaze removal + seasoning verification. Weathered: chemical restoration protocol (strip → brighten → neutralize). Previously_coated: assess existing coating integrity, strip if failing, sand if sound. Each condition has fundamentally different prep time and materials.
condition_drivers.notes: This spec is NOT NC-only — it covers all three wood conditions. The 'v1' name deliberately omits NC. This is RC-001.

condition_drivers.impact: Drives prep chemistry (oxalic acid brightener for cedar/redwood tannin), seasoning time (PT pine 3-6 months, cedar/redwood shorter), tannin bleed risk (cedar/redwood high), and stain compatibility (oil-based resists tannin bleed better on cedar/redwood). Composite EXCLUDED per RC-004.
condition_drivers.notes: PT pine is ~80% of residential decks. Cedar and redwood are premium substrates with tannin management requirements.

condition_drivers.impact: Spray_backbrush is the production method for deck floors (fastest for large areas). Brush is the primary method for railings, spindles, and detail work. Roll can be used on floor field but has lower penetration than brush. Pad applicator (lamb's wool or synthetic) is used for smooth floor application of penetrating stains. IMPORTANT: spray on deck = ALWAYS add back-brush (not backroll).
condition_drivers.notes: spray_backbrush is the deck equivalent of masonry spray_backroll. Brush back-working forces stain into wood grain.

condition_drivers.impact: Ground-level decks (on-grade or within 2 ft of grade) have minimal below-deck concerns. Elevated decks (4+ ft above grade) require below-deck overspray protection for landscaping and have access considerations for underside staining if specified. Most residential decks are ground-level or low-elevated.
condition_drivers.notes: Deck height affects protection scope, not production rate (work is performed from the deck surface, not from ladders). Height modifier does NOT apply to deck floor staining — crew stands on the surface being stained.

condition_drivers.impact: Drives which paintable items are active. Floor_only: deck floor field only (most common maintenance recoat). Floor_and_railings: floor + railing system (no stairs or separate stair pricing). Full_deck: floor + railings + spindles + stairs (new construction or full restoration). Each component has distinct production rates.
condition_drivers.notes: This is a SCOPE DIMENSION that controls item activation, similar to cabinet scope (doors_only/full_exterior/full_with_interior).

quality_differences.description: Economy/minimal protection. No UV pigment — wood grain fully visible, natural appearance. Water repellent only. 12-18 month maintenance cycle (annual recoat). Fastest to apply. Lowest material cost. No color matching required. Best for: cedar/redwood where natural wood color is desired.
quality_differences.typical_use: Homeowners who want natural wood look. Cedar and redwood decks. Annual maintenance commitment required.

quality_differences.description: PROFESSIONAL STANDARD. Pigmented penetrating stain — wood grain visible through color. UV protection from pigment. 2-3 year maintenance cycle. Good balance of aesthetics, protection, and maintainability. Easy maintenance recoat (clean and recoat, no stripping). Most forgiving application — penetrating stain hides minor application inconsistencies.
quality_differences.typical_use: Standard residential deck staining. Most contractor-recommended option. ~60% of professional deck staining work.

quality_differences.description: Heavy-pigment penetrating stain. Partially masks wood grain — texture visible but grain pattern obscured. 3-4 year maintenance cycle. Better UV and wear protection than semi-transparent. Useful for hiding wood imperfections, color inconsistencies, or previous stain color underneath.
quality_differences.typical_use: Decks with cosmetic wood defects. Color change over previous stain. Homeowners wanting longer maintenance cycle than semi-transparent.

quality_differences.description: Film-forming coating (essentially paint). Complete grain masking — opaque color. 5-7 year cycle on vertical surfaces but DELAMINATION RISK on horizontal walking surfaces. Requires more prep for recoat (sand, possibly strip). Tannin-blocking primer may be required on cedar/redwood. Closest to traditional paint behavior. MANDATORY WARNING: document delamination risk on horizontal deck surfaces.
quality_differences.typical_use: Color matching to house trim. Covering severely weathered or stained wood. Homeowner prioritizes longevity over wood appearance. Vertical railing components only (safer application).

failure_modes.name: Film delamination from moisture entrapment (solid stain on horizontal)
failure_modes.description: Solid stain forms a film on horizontal deck surfaces that traps moisture from rain, snow, and irrigation entering through cracks, end-grain, and fastener holes. Water becomes trapped between wood and film, causing blistering and sheet delamination. Foot traffic accelerates film failure. This is the most common and most severe deck coating failure mode.
failure_modes.prevention: Use penetrating stains (semi-transparent or semi-solid) on horizontal walking surfaces. If solid stain is specified, document risk warning. Ensure all fastener holes and end-grain are sealed. Verify MC < 15% before application.
failure_modes.detection: Blistering or bubbling of stain film. Sheets of coating lifting off surface. White/gray patches where film has separated. Soft, pliable film when pressed.

failure_modes.name: Premature erosion from insufficient penetration
failure_modes.description: Penetrating stain applied to wood with mill glaze, excess moisture (MC > 15%), or insufficient surface preparation fails to penetrate into wood fibers. Stain sits on the surface and erodes within weeks/months instead of the expected 2-3 year cycle. Most common on new PT pine that has not been properly seasoned or prepped.
failure_modes.prevention: Remove mill glaze on all new wood (chemical or 60-80 grit sanding). Verify MC < 15%. Verify PT pine has seasoned 3-6 months. Perform water absorption test. Back-brush when spraying to force stain into grain.
failure_modes.detection: Rapid color loss within first season. Bare wood showing through stain within 6 months. Uneven wear patterns indicating inconsistent penetration.

failure_modes.name: Tannin bleed-through on cedar/redwood
failure_modes.description: Water-soluble extractive tannins in cedar and redwood bleed through coatings, causing dark brown/red discoloration. Most severe with water-based coatings and at end-grain locations. Tannin bleed stains surrounding surfaces (concrete, siding) and discolors the coating itself.
failure_modes.prevention: Treat cedar/redwood with oxalic acid brightener before staining to dissolve surface tannins. Consider oil-based stain for cedar/redwood (better tannin resistance). For solid stain, use tannin-blocking primer. Accept some tannin bleed as normal with clear/semi-transparent coatings on cedar.
failure_modes.detection: Dark brown/reddish streaks or blotches through stain. Staining of adjacent concrete or siding below deck. Most visible after rain events.

failure_modes.name: Alligatoring / checking on over-applied coatings
failure_modes.description: Excessive stain application (too much product, insufficient back-brushing, or applying before previous coat absorbs) creates a thick surface film on what should be a penetrating coating. The thick film cracks in a pattern resembling alligator skin as wood expands and contracts. Common on end-grain areas that absorb unevenly.
failure_modes.prevention: Apply thin coats. Maintain wet edge. Back-brush thoroughly to work stain into wood. Do not allow puddles or pooling. Apply second coat only after first coat has absorbed (typically 30-60 minutes for penetrating stains). Watch end-grain application rate.
failure_modes.detection: Network of fine cracks in a grid/scale pattern on coating surface. Thick, shiny film visible on what should be a matte penetrating finish. Most apparent on end-grain and joints.

failure_modes.name: Mildew and biological growth under/through coating
failure_modes.description: Deck surfaces in shaded, humid areas develop mildew and algae growth on or under the coating. Horizontal surfaces retain moisture longer than vertical. North-facing decks and shaded areas under tree canopy are highest risk. Mildew grows on the coating surface (cosmetic) or under film-forming coatings (structural).
failure_modes.prevention: Use stain products with mildewcide additive. Ensure proper deck drainage (no standing water). Clean deck annually. Pre-treat with mildew cleaner before staining. Address surrounding vegetation for air circulation.
failure_modes.detection: Black, green, or gray spots/patches on coating surface. Musty odor. Slippery surface when wet.

failure_modes.name: Freeze-thaw shearing on saturated wood
failure_modes.description: Water absorbed into wood fibers freezes and expands (~9%), mechanically shearing wood fibers and breaking coating bond. Horizontal deck surfaces are most vulnerable because water pools and soaks in from above while ground moisture wicks from below. Film-forming coatings (solid stain) trap moisture and worsen freeze-thaw damage.
failure_modes.prevention: Use penetrating stains that allow moisture vapor transmission. Verify MC < 15% before staining. Ensure deck drainage (proper board spacing, slight slope). Avoid solid stain in freeze-thaw climates where possible.
failure_modes.detection: Rough, fuzzy wood surface where fibers have been lifted. Coating flaking in small patches at fiber separation points. Most visible in spring after freeze-thaw cycles.

notes_for_materials_manager: This is a STAIN spec, not a paint spec. Primary materials are penetrating stains, not paints. Material system branches by coating_type: clear_sealer, semi_transparent, semi_solid, solid_stain.

Penetrating stains (clear, semi-transparent, semi-solid) do NOT use primer. Primer would seal wood surface and prevent stain penetration. Only solid stain may require primer on previously coated surfaces or cedar/redwood (tannin block).

Coverage rates vary by wood porosity and condition: new smooth wood 200-300 SF/gal, weathered/porous wood 150-250 SF/gal, end-grain areas consume 2-3x normal rate. Penetrating stains typically 200-350 SF/gal. Solid stain 300-400 SF/gal (film-forming, less absorption).

Cedar/redwood substrates: oxalic acid brightener (powder, mix on-site) for tannin treatment. Oil-based stain recommended for better tannin resistance. If water-based stain is specified on cedar/redwood, document tannin bleed risk.

Weathered wood prep materials: sodium percarbonate or sodium hydroxide-based deck cleaner (alkaline strip), oxalic acid or citric acid brightener (acid step), stiff synthetic bristle brushes for back-brushing.

Spray application back-brushing: stiff synthetic bristle brush (not roller). 4-6 inch brush for floor field, 2-3 inch brush for railings and detail. Replace brushes frequently — stain degrades bristles faster than paint.
Solid stain on cedar/redwood may require tannin-blocking primer (shellac-based or specialty exterior tannin block). This is the ONLY primer scenario in this spec.
Stain products with mildewcide additive recommended for all deck applications (horizontal surfaces retain moisture). Standard product line should include mildewcide versions.

Masking materials: plastic sheeting (4-6 mil) for siding protection during spray, painter's tape for trim interfaces. Red stucco poly tape NOT needed (deck surfaces are smooth wood, not rough masonry).
notes_for_sop_librarian: Module structure: setup → protect → clean/strip → prep → stain_apply → cleanup → teardown. Note: NO prime module for penetrating stains (clear/semi-transparent/semi-solid). Prime module only for solid stain on cedar/redwood or previously coated.
Seasoning verification task is FIRST for new PT pine — must verify 3-6 month age and MC < 15%. HARD STOP if wood is less than 3 months old.
Moisture testing (MC < 15%) is mandatory before stain application on ALL wood conditions. Pin-type electronic moisture meter. Water bead test as field supplement.
Mill glaze removal is mandatory on all new wood substrates. Chemical mill glaze remover (preferred, brush-on, wait, rinse) or mechanical sanding (60-80 grit). This is a prep task before staining.

Weathered wood chemical restoration is a 3-step conditional module: (1) alkaline strip/clean, (2) acid brighten (oxalic for cedar/redwood, citric alternative), (3) neutralize and rinse. Allow 24-48 hours drying after chemical restoration before staining.

Previously coated wood: assess existing coating. Sound penetrating stain: clean and recoat directly. Failed penetrating stain: light sand, clean, recoat. Sound solid stain: light sand for adhesion, recoat. Failed solid stain: full strip to bare wood, then treat as weathered.

Spray on deck = ALWAYS add back-brush task. Spray deposits stain on surface; back-brushing with stiff bristle brush forces stain into wood pores. This is MANDATORY for penetrating stains. Similar concept to masonry backroll but uses brush, not roller.

Floor field staining sequence: work from far end toward exit. Maintain wet edge. Do not allow laps. Apply second coat of penetrating stain after first coat absorbs (30-60 minutes typically). Do NOT let second coat dry on surface — back-brush any pooling.
Railing and spindle staining: brush application primary method. Spray railing runs then back-brush. Spindles individually brushed — high labor intensity.
Stairs: stain every other step, allow to dry, then stain remaining steps (maintains access throughout). Each tread+riser is one unit (EA).
Solid stain on horizontal deck: MANDATORY risk documentation. Document delamination risk warning in project record. Recommend semi-transparent or semi-solid as alternative.

Environmental SOP note: stain application when surface temp is 50-90°F. Avoid direct sun on surface during application (causes flash drying and uneven absorption). Early morning or overcast preferred.
notes_for_estimation_engineer: Production rates by component — Floor field: staining 200-350 SF/hr (brush/pad), spray_backbrush 300-450 SF/hr. Sanding 40-60 SF/hr. Chemical restoration (full 3-step): 80-120 SF/hr.
Railings: 10-15 LF/hr (brush application, includes top rail, bottom rail, posts per linear foot). Spray_backbrush railings: 15-25 LF/hr.
Spindles/balusters: 10-20 EA/hr (individually brushed). High labor intensity — each spindle has 4 sides plus top/bottom. Turned spindles slower than square.
Stairs: 2-4 steps/hr (EA — each tread+riser is one unit). Includes end-grain sealing, detail brushwork. Alternating step pattern adds scheduling overhead.
Mill glaze removal: chemical 100-150 SF/hr (apply, wait, rinse). Mechanical sanding 40-60 SF/hr (60-80 grit).

Weathered wood chemical restoration (3-step): 80-120 SF/hr total (strip application + wait + rinse, brightener application + wait + rinse, final rinse). 24-48 hour dry time between restoration and staining — this is a separate mobilization or multi-day schedule.
Moisture testing: fixed time per project (~0.5-1.0 hr). Pin-type meter readings at multiple locations. Water bead test supplemental.
Back-brushing rate is embedded in spray_backbrush rate (not a separate line item). Two-person crew: one sprays, one back-brushes immediately behind.
Solid stain application rates are similar to paint (300-400 SF/hr spray_backbrush on floor). Film-forming application, not penetrating.

Coat system: penetrating stains typically 2 coats (apply, let absorb, apply second while first is still workable OR after short absorption period). Solid stain: 2 coats with full dry between. Clear sealer: 1-2 coats depending on product.
Environmental conditions (wind, dew point, sun, temp) are EXCLUDED from estimation — they are SOP/process concerns, not estimatable at bid time. Per established exterior spec convention.
On-deck furniture staging: count as protection EA items. Move furniture off deck or consolidate and cover. 10-20 min per furniture group.
Below-deck vegetation protection: LF along deck perimeter for elevated decks. Ground-level decks have minimal below-deck concern.

assumptions.value: Deck staining/coating — horizontal walking surface + railings + stairs. Covers new construction AND existing/maintenance. Exterior horizontal wood surfaces only.
assumptions.note: This spec covers BOTH NC and existing decks. Wood_condition dimension handles new vs weathered vs previously_coated. Spec name is SF_DECK_EXT_v1 (no NC in name).

assumptions.value: coating_type is the primary configuration dimension. No traditional QT2-QT5 quality tier dimension.
assumptions.note: Deck coating selection maps loosely to quality level: clear_sealer ≈ economy, semi_transparent ≈ standard, semi_solid ≈ enhanced, solid_stain ≈ premium. But the mapping is imperfect — coating_type drives fundamentally different chemistry and failure profiles, not just scrutiny level.

assumptions.value: Composite decking (Trex, TimberTech, Fiberon) excluded from primary scope.
assumptions.note: Composite is maintenance-free by design. Manufacturer warranties void if coated. Edge case only — would require separate adhesion protocol if ever needed.

assumptions.value: Mandatory back-brushing on all spray-applied penetrating stains. No spray-only option for penetrating stains on decks.
assumptions.note: Similar to masonry backroll but uses stiff bristle brush instead of roller. Brush action forces stain into wood grain pores.

assumptions.value: Penetrating stains (clear, semi-transparent, semi-solid) do NOT use primer. Primer blocks stain penetration.
assumptions.note: This breaks the standard prime→paint pipeline. Only solid stain on cedar/redwood or previously painted surfaces may require primer.

assumptions.value: Deck stairs counted as EA (per step — each tread+riser is one unit), not LF.
assumptions.note: Each step is a discrete work unit with consistent labor regardless of step width (typical 36-48 inch residential stair width).

uncertainties.detail: Pad applicators (lamb's wool or synthetic) are a common deck staining tool for floor field but production rates are not explicitly provided in doctrine. Industry practice suggests rates similar to brush (200-300 SF/hr) with potentially smoother finish.
uncertainties.recommendation: Use brush rate as baseline for pad applicator. Flag for field calibration.

uncertainties.topic: Oil-based vs water-based stain rate difference
uncertainties.detail: Doctrine provides general production rates but does not differentiate between oil-based and water-based stain application rates. Oil-based stains have longer open time (easier wet edge maintenance) but slower dry time. Water-based stains dry faster (can do two coats same day in ideal conditions).
uncertainties.recommendation: Use same production rate for both. Note oil-based advantage for wet edge on large floor areas. Flag for field calibration.

uncertainties.topic: Chemical restoration 24-48 hour dry time impact on scheduling
uncertainties.detail: Weathered wood chemical restoration requires 24-48 hours drying before staining. This may require a separate mobilization day, which adds scheduling overhead and potential additional mobilization cost not captured in per-SF production rates.
uncertainties.recommendation: Flag multi-day scheduling for weathered wood restoration as a project-level note. Chemical restoration and staining are effectively separate mobilizations.

uncertainties.detail: Spindle count per LF of railing varies by design — typical 4-inch on-center spacing yields ~3 spindles per LF, but wider spacing and decorative patterns vary. PaintScope may need a spindle count input or a derivation from railing LF.
uncertainties.recommendation: Propose PS key for spindle count (EA). If not available, derive from railing LF using 3 spindles/LF default with override capability.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray_backbrush
zones.notes: House siding at deck-to-house junction. Brush application: tape at ledger board. Spray: plastic sheeting on siding face from deck level up 4-6 ft.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray_backbrush
zones.notes: Vegetation and landscaping below elevated deck. Drop cloth/tarp below deck perimeter. Ground-level decks have minimal below-deck concern.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_cover when application_method = spray_backbrush
zones.notes: Walkways, patios, concrete pads adjacent to deck at ground level. Drop cloth runners or plastic sheeting.
On-deck furniture, planters, grills. Move off deck entirely (preferred) or consolidate and cover with plastic. Not a masking task — relocation/staging.
Deck-mounted or railing-mounted light fixtures. Bag or tape over fixture during staining.

protection_zones_analysis.cross_spec_protection_note: Door protection at deck-to-house entry is NOT this spec's responsibility. Door masking belongs in the door spec. Siding protection at the ledger board junction IS this spec's responsibility because stain overspray/drip from deck work contacts siding.

adjacent_surfaces.notes: House siding at ledger board junction. Deck stain terminates at house wall. Protection required to prevent stain contact with siding. No cut-in — different product systems entirely.
Railing system mounted on deck perimeter. Same stain product typically. Separate paintable item within this spec (LF-based). No edge work — components are stained separately.
Stair treads/risers connecting deck to grade. Same stain product. Separate paintable item within this spec (EA-based). Junction requires careful wet-edge management.
Foundation visible below elevated deck. Not in scope. Below-deck protection zones handle overspray.
Entry door at deck-to-house junction. Different product system. Door protection owned by door spec.

adjacency_analysis.key_finding: Deck floor field has NO edge work within this spec. Adjacent siding/door are different product systems (stain vs paint) with protection-only relationship. Railing and stairs are separate paintable items within this spec, stained with same product but counted/rated independently.

affected_conditions.notes: Access modifier applies ONLY to railing/spindle work on elevated decks where crew must work from ladder to reach railing exterior face. Floor staining has NO height modifier — crew stands on the surface. Scaffold and lift are extremely rare for residential deck railings.
MC > 15% prevents stain penetration. Hard stop. Reschedule. Electronic pin-type moisture meter is authoritative measurement.

excluded_conditions.rationale: Environmental conditions are important to the staining PROCESS but are NOT estimatable. They are unpredictable, change daily, and cannot be set as fixed conditions for an estimate. Per established exterior spec convention.

excluded.reason: Unpredictable. Changes hourly. Cannot set a fixed modifier for estimate.
Varies by time of day, sun angle, and season. Not predictable at bid time.
Weather-dependent. Not predictable at bid time.
Direct sun causes flash drying of stain. Scheduling concern, not estimation.

valid_input_states.rationale: Three input states correspond to the three wood_condition values. SS_EXT_BARE_WOOD = new wood (PT pine, cedar, redwood) awaiting first coat. SS_EXT_STAINED = previously stained wood with existing coating (sound or failing). SS_EXT_WEATHERED = UV-degraded, grayed wood with lost or eroded coating requiring chemical restoration.

output_state.rationale: All coating types produce a stained output state. Clear sealer produces SS_EXT_SEALED (sub-variant). Semi-transparent, semi-solid, and solid stain all produce SS_EXT_STAINED. Output state determines maintenance recoat approach.

adjacent_state_protection_analysis.rationale: Stain overspray on finished siding is difficult to remove (penetrating product absorbs into painted surface). Full cover for finished siding. Even unfinished siding gets light masking because stain discolors bare wood differently than intended siding finish.
Door at deck entry point. Stain splatter on door finish is visible and hard to remove. Protection owned by door spec, but deck spec must avoid contact.
Foundation below deck is rarely visible. Below-deck protection zones cover overspray for elevated decks.

exterior_substrate_states.description: New, uncoated wood deck surface. Pressure-treated pine, cedar, or redwood. May have mill glaze from sawmill planing. PT pine requires 3-6 month seasoning before staining.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Verify seasoning (PT pine: 3-6 months, HARD STOP if < 3 months). Moisture test (MC < 15% mandatory). Mill glaze removal (chemical or 60-80 grit sanding). Water absorption test to verify readiness.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: None — penetrating stains do not use primer. Exception: solid stain on cedar/redwood may require tannin-blocking primer.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: New wood condition. Most common for new construction decks. PT pine is ~80% of residential decks.

exterior_substrate_states.description: Previously stained wood deck surface with existing penetrating or film-forming coating. Coating may be sound (maintenance recoat) or failing (requires strip/sand).
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Assess existing coating integrity. Sound penetrating stain: clean and recoat. Failed penetrating stain: light sand, clean, recoat. Sound solid stain: light sand for adhesion profile, recoat. Failed solid stain: full strip to bare wood, then treat as weathered.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: None for penetrating stain recoat. Solid stain over different product type may require adhesion primer.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Previously coated condition. Prep requirements vary dramatically by existing coating type and condition.

exterior_substrate_states.description: UV-degraded, grayed wood with lost or severely eroded coating. Loose wood fibers, silvery-gray color from lignin photodegradation. May have mildew, algae, or dirt accumulation.
exterior_substrate_states.prep_requirements: Full chemical restoration protocol: (1) alkaline strip/clean, (2) acid brighten (oxalic acid for cedar/redwood), (3) neutralize and rinse. Allow 24-48 hours drying. Verify MC < 15% after drying. May require light sanding (80-100 grit) to remove remaining loose fibers.
exterior_substrate_states.primer_type: None — penetrating stains applied directly to restored bare wood.
exterior_substrate_states.notes: Weathered condition is the most labor-intensive prep. Chemical restoration is a multi-step process requiring 24-48 hour dry time before staining.

exterior_access_type_analysis.treatment: Modifier on railing/spindle tasks only. Floor staining has NO height modifier — crew stands on deck surface.

scenarios.notes: Standard deck railing work. Crew stands on deck surface. All floor staining is ground-level by definition.
Exterior face of elevated deck railings where crew must reach from ladder or from ground below. Rare — most railing work is from deck surface.

exterior_access_type_analysis.key_distinction: Unlike masonry or siding specs, deck work is performed FROM the surface being stained. Height modifier only applies to the limited scenario of staining the exterior face of elevated deck railings from below.

exterior_environmental_constraints.note: Environmental constraints are documented here for SOP reference but are EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers per established exterior spec convention.

sop_reference_only.note: Below 50: stain won't penetrate properly, slow cure. Above 90: flash drying, uneven absorption, lap marks.

sop_reference_only.rule: Surface temp must be >= 5°F above dew point
sop_reference_only.note: Morning dew on deck surfaces — wait until surface is dry.
Pin-type electronic moisture meter. Water bead test as field supplement.

sop_reference_only.rule: Avoid staining in direct sun — causes flash drying and uneven absorption
sop_reference_only.note: Schedule for early morning, late afternoon, or overcast. Stain shaded sections first, sun-exposed sections when shade arrives.

sop_reference_only.rule: No stain application if rain within 24-48 hours (product-dependent)
sop_reference_only.note: Penetrating stains need dry time to cure in wood fibers. Rain washes uncured stain from surface.

sop_reference_only.rule: PT pine: minimum 3 months seasoning (HARD STOP). 6 months preferred.
sop_reference_only.note: Not a daily condition but a project-level gate. Verify with builder/GC.

floor_stain_brush.notes: Brush or pad applicator on deck floor field. Penetrating stain. Higher end on smooth new wood, lower on rough/weathered.

floor_stain_spray_backbrush.notes: Spray + immediate back-brush. 2-person crew. Fastest method for large deck floors. Penetrating stain.

floor_stain_solid_spray_backbrush.notes: Solid stain (film-forming) spray + back-brush. Similar to paint application rate.

floor_sanding.notes: Deck floor sanding (60-80 grit for mill glaze, 80-100 grit for weathered fiber removal). Random orbital or belt sander.

railing_stain_brush.notes: Brush application on railings. Includes top rail, bottom rail, posts per LF. Detail work.

spindle_stain_brush.notes: Individual spindle/baluster staining. 4 sides + top/bottom per spindle. Turned spindles at lower end.

stair_stain.notes: Per step (tread+riser = 1 EA). Includes end-grain sealing and detail brushwork.

mill_glaze_removal_chemical.notes: Chemical mill glaze remover: apply, wait (15-30 min), rinse. New wood only.

mill_glaze_removal_sand.notes: Mechanical sanding for mill glaze. 60-80 grit. Same rate as general floor sanding.

chemical_restoration_full.notes: Full 3-step weathered wood restoration: strip + brighten + neutralize. Includes application, wait times, rinsing. 24-48 hr dry time after.

moisture_testing.notes: Fixed time per project. Pin-type meter readings at multiple locations across deck surface.

furniture_staging.notes: Move/consolidate on-deck furniture. Per furniture group or section.

power_wash_existing.notes: Low-pressure wash for previously coated or dirty deck. Fan tip, 1200-1500 PSI max (higher pressure damages wood fibers).

key_decisions.decision: This spec uses coating_type as primary dimension instead of quality_tier. No traditional QT2-QT5 axis.
key_decisions.rationale: Deck coating selection drives fundamentally different chemistry (penetrating vs film-forming), failure modes (erosion vs delamination), maintenance cycles (1-7 years), and primer requirements (none vs possible). Quality tier scrutiny differences are secondary to coating chemistry. RC-003.

key_decisions.topic: NC and existing decks in one spec
key_decisions.decision: This spec covers all wood conditions: new, weathered, previously_coated. Not NC-only.
key_decisions.rationale: Wood_condition dimension handles prep module selection. The core staining workflow is the same regardless of wood condition — only prep differs. Splitting into NC vs maintenance specs would duplicate 80% of content. RC-001.

key_decisions.decision: Four paintable items: deck_floor_field (SF), deck_railing (LF), deck_spindle (EA), deck_stair_step (EA).
key_decisions.rationale: Each component has dramatically different production rates, counting methods, and access conditions. Floor field is the primary item. Railings, spindles, and stairs are optional scope components activated by the scope_components dimension.

key_decisions.decision: Composite decking EXCLUDED from primary scope.
key_decisions.rationale: Composite is maintenance-free by design. Manufacturer warranties void if coated. Not a standard painting contractor scope. Edge case only. RC-004.

key_decisions.topic: Spray always includes back-brush for penetrating stains
key_decisions.decision: Application method 'spray_backbrush' is a single unit for penetrating stains. No spray-only option.
key_decisions.rationale: Spray deposits stain on surface but does not force it into wood pores. Back-brushing with stiff bristle brush is MANDATORY for penetrating stain penetration. Similar concept to masonry backroll but uses brush. RC-005.

key_decisions.topic: No primer module for penetrating stains
key_decisions.decision: Penetrating stains (clear, semi-transparent, semi-solid) have NO prime module. Stain applies directly to prepared wood.
key_decisions.rationale: Primer seals wood surface and prevents stain penetration. The traditional prime→paint pipeline does not apply. Only solid stain on cedar/redwood or previously painted may require tannin-blocking or adhesion primer as an exception.

key_decisions.decision: Solid stain on horizontal deck surfaces triggers MANDATORY risk documentation in project record.
key_decisions.rationale: Film-forming coatings on horizontal walking surfaces have documented high delamination risk from moisture entrapment. Professional recommendation is semi-transparent or semi-solid for horizontal. If solid stain is specified, risk must be documented.

key_decisions.topic: Stairs counted as EA per step
key_decisions.decision: Deck stairs counted as EA (each tread+riser = 1 unit), not LF.
key_decisions.rationale: Each step is a discrete work unit with consistent labor regardless of width. RC-007.

key_decisions.decision: EXCLUDED from estimation modifiers. Per established exterior spec convention.
key_decisions.rationale: Environmental conditions are unpredictable at bid time. They are SOP/process concerns documented for field reference but not included in production rate modifiers.

key_decisions.decision: Height/access modifier applies ONLY to exterior railing face work on elevated decks. Floor staining has no height modifier.
key_decisions.rationale: Deck floor staining is performed by crew standing ON the deck surface — there is no elevation premium. Height modifier only applies to the rare scenario of staining the exterior face of elevated deck railings from below.

key_decisions.decision: Weathered wood chemical restoration and staining are effectively separate mobilizations due to 24-48 hour dry time.
key_decisions.rationale: Chemical restoration (strip → brighten → neutralize) requires 24-48 hours drying before stain can be applied. This creates a multi-day scheduling requirement that may affect project pricing.

key_decisions.decision: Include scope_components dimension: floor_only, floor_and_railings, full_deck.
key_decisions.rationale: Controls which paintable items are active. Maintenance recoats often address floor only. New construction is typically full deck. Similar pattern to cabinet scope (doors_only/full_exterior/full_with_interior).

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Primary configuration dimension for deck spec. Drives coating chemistry, primer requirement, failure mode profile, and maintenance cycle. Not captured by existing PS keys.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Project-level setting. Replaces quality_tier as the primary dimension for deck staining.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Drives prep module selection. Each condition has fundamentally different prep time and materials.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Project-level setting. Determines which prep tasks are activated.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Drives prep chemistry (oxalic acid for cedar/redwood), seasoning requirements (PT pine), and stain compatibility.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Project-level setting. PT pine is ~80% of residential decks.

proposed_new_keys.rationale: Count of on-deck furniture groups requiring relocation/covering. Unique to deck scope — no equivalent in wall/siding specs.
proposed_new_keys.notes: Furniture staging is a protection task unique to decks (items ON the surface being stained).

research_corrections.original_assumption: Spec covers new construction only (NC pattern from sibling specs)
research_corrections.corrected_to: Spec covers BOTH NC and existing decks. Wood_condition dimension handles new vs weathered vs previously_coated.
research_corrections.rationale: The spec name is SF_DECK_EXT_v1 (no NC in name). Unlike masonry or siding where NC vs repaint require fundamentally different coating systems, deck staining uses the same products on all wood conditions — only prep differs.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Environmental conditions might be estimatable for outdoor decks
research_corrections.corrected_to: Environmental conditions EXCLUDED from estimation per established exterior spec convention.
research_corrections.rationale: Same convention as masonry and siding siblings. Environmental conditions are unpredictable at bid time.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Standard QT2-QT5 quality tier dimension applies
research_corrections.corrected_to: coating_type is the primary configuration dimension. No traditional quality tier.
research_corrections.rationale: Coating type drives fundamentally different chemistry, failure modes, and maintenance expectations. Quality tier scrutiny (inspection at 3ft vs 6ft) is secondary and largely irrelevant for stain application (no lap marks, drips, or film defects to inspect for on penetrating stains).

research_corrections.original_assumption: Composite decking included in substrate types
research_corrections.corrected_to: Composite EXCLUDED from primary scope. Edge case only.
research_corrections.rationale: Composite is maintenance-free by design. Manufacturer warranties void if coated. Not standard painting contractor scope.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Spray backroll pattern from masonry/siding applies
research_corrections.corrected_to: Spray back-BRUSH for penetrating stains. Brush forces stain into wood pores. Roller does not provide same bristle action for stain penetration.
research_corrections.rationale: Different substrate physics. Masonry backroll forces paint film into void pores. Wood back-brush forces penetrating stain into grain channels. Similar concept, different tool and technique.

research_corrections.original_assumption: Standard exterior landscape/hardscape protection zones apply
research_corrections.corrected_to: Deck has unique protection profile: siding at ledger board (always), below-deck vegetation (elevated only), on-deck furniture (when present). Less landscape concern than wall painting (deck is elevated).
research_corrections.rationale: Deck is an elevated platform, not a wall. Landscape protection is below-deck (drip-through), not at-grade (wall overspray). On-deck furniture staging is unique to deck scope.

research_corrections.corrected_to: Stairs counted as EA (per step — each tread+riser = 1 unit).
research_corrections.rationale: Each step is a discrete work unit with consistent labor per step regardless of stair width. LF would not capture the per-step detail work accurately.
